item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] Why Greece's alliances failed to prevent eastern Libya's maritime deal with Turkey
item.description:
Why Greece's alliances failed to prevent eastern Libya's maritime deal with Turkey

Submitted by Sean Mathews on Tue, 10/20/2026 - 21:39
Egypt and Turkey cohere on several hotspots while Gulf states seek new security partners, and Israel's interests are served by supporting Saddam Haftar's rise to power
Libyan strongman Khalifa Haftar (L) speaks with Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis during talks in Athens, on 17 January 2020 (Aris Messinis/AFP)
Off

In the days before Libya’s eastern parliament approved a contentious maritime agreement with Turkey, Greece was trying to assemble its allies - Egypt, Israel and the UAE - to prevent the deal, multiple officials in the region told Middle East Eye.

But on Tuesday, the Libyan House of Representatives in Benghazi ratified the agreement, showing that a fractured Libya, at the very least, could come to a consensus in acknowledging Turkey’s sweeping maritime claims over the Eastern Mediterranean.

“Turkey has cemented itself in Libya. It’s almost impossible now for a Libyan leader in the future to sign a deal with Greece because there is a Libyan consensus,” Constantinos Filis, director of the Institute of Global Affairs in Athens, told Middle East Eye.

But the deal is more than a setback for Greece or a diplomatic notch in the belt for the Mediterranean. It underscores how the Middle East is rearranging itself in the wake of the US-Israeli war on Iran and simmering conflicts across the region.

In sum, the partnerships that Greece depended on to counter Turkey in the Mediterranean failed to deliver because the Middle East is undergoing a geopolitical reordering of priorities. 

Egypt and Turkey have mended fences after a deep rift, while Gulf states like the UAE are looking for new security partners, with the Iran war on the verge of flaring up again. The irony for Greece is that the actions of its closest partner, Israel, have contributed to these shifts.

US vacuum

The maritime rivalry between Greece and Turkey in the Eastern Mediterranean long predates the fracturing of Libya into rival governments following the 2011 removal of Muammar Gaddafi. The two neighbours came close to war in 1996 over an uninhabited island.

Traditionally, Greece and Turkey could push the envelope in their tensions, knowing that the US would intervene to prevent its Nato allies from crossing the line into direct conflict. But that dynamic has changed.

The US is now less engaged in the Middle East and is at loggerheads with Nato on several fronts, like the war in Ukraine. Greece is a big spender in Nato, but Turkey has developed a domestic weapons industry of its own.

Turkey’s regional power is increasing, with an ally now governing Syria and Gulf states looking to it as a security partner as the US steps away.

Tom Barrack, the US ambassador to Turkey and envoy to Syria and Iraq, said on Tuesday that the US's  “grand bargain” of oil for security with the Gulf was “transitioning”.

A Libyan source familiar with the matter told Middle East Eye that eastern Libya’s ratification of the maritime deal is one step in a wider plan to unite Libya under one government that the Trump administration has agreed to with Turkey. The source said the US wants Turkey to broker a deal between rival governments in Benghazi and Tripoli. Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin visited the latter on Tuesday.

Greece has sought new Middle Eastern allies as the US retreats from its security role, and Turkey flexes its muscles in the region. The maritime deal Ankara has with Libya disregards Greek claims to maritime zones not just in uninhabited islands, but large ones like Crete, home to 600,000 Greeks.

Greece's search for allies to fill the US gap

Athens has doubled down on its relatively warm, historic ties to Egypt. When Turkey first signed the maritime demarcation deal with Libya’s Tripoli-based government, Athens responded by signing a deal with Egypt to counter it.

Greece has also moved closer to the UAE. Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis was one of the first foreign leaders to visit the Gulf state at the height of the US-Israeli war on Iran. In 2020, when tensions between Greece and Turkey soared, the UAE sent warplanes to Crete.

The New Byzantines: An exploration of Greece's Middle East ties, which are resurfacing in a turbulent world
Read More »

But most controversially, Greece has forged a close alliance with Israel, which is clashing with Turkey for power in hotspots like Syria and even the Horn of Africa. In August, Greece even agreed to purchase a $3.5bn air defence system from Israel - the largest arms deal in Israel’s history.

Eastern Libya’s ratification of the Turkish maritime deal stings especially hard for Greece because Israel, Egypt and the UAE are the main backers of Khalifa Haftar, the military commander who controls eastern Libya and has traditionally been a rival to Libya’s Tripoli-based government.

Greece has leaned on these relationships to try to counter Turkey in Libya.

In 2025, Greece sought Egyptian support to forestall Benghazi’s ratification of the maritime deal. An Egyptian delegation visited Athens just five days ago to confer with Greece on Libya.

Khalifa Haftar’s son, Saddam Haftar, is increasingly seen as the next ruler of eastern Libya. Although Turkey intervened in Libya’s civil war to prevent his father from capturing Tripoli, Saddam has moved closer to Ankara. This summer, with some nudging from the UAE, Saddam was convinced to visit Athens despite his rapprochement with Turkey, MEE understands.

“It’s not up to Egypt or the UAE to support us in Libya. They have other interests. It was unwise for Greece to expect that they would support Greece at the sake of their own interests,” Filis told MEE.

Turkey and Egypt's rapprochement

Until a few years ago, both Egypt and the UAE were at loggerheads with Turkey. Cairo and Abu Dhabi supported the Haftars in Libya’s civil war, while Turkey backed the government in Tripoli. But since then, these countries have taken steps to restore ties.

Egyptian officials have stressed multiple times to MEE that Cairo’s rapprochement is not aimed at Greece. Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty held a call with his Greek counterpart on Tuesday, reaffirming their shared interests.

Greece's alliance with Israel is becoming a domestic liability

Egypt does not want to see the Eastern Mediterranean turned into a Turkish lake, Arab officials tell MEE, but Egypt and Turkey now converge in more hotspots than they compete.

Both countries are wary of Israeli expansionism in the wake of the Hamas-led 7 October 2023 attacks. Israel has carried out a genocide in Gaza and occupies swathes of Syria and Lebanon.

Egypt and Turkey are also aligned in the Red Sea. Both states support Somalia and oppose Israel’s recognition of a breakaway Somaliland republic. They also support Sudan’s armed forces against the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) paramilitary, which is friendly to Israel, by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s own admission.

In Libya, there is also room for cooperation. Egypt wants to build a $1bn oil pipeline from Tobruk to the port of Alexandria.

While the UAE and Turkey are on opposite sides of these regional hotspots like Sudan, they have since moved to manage their differences. For example, in 2022, the UAE purchased Turkish-made TB2 drones. 

Then there is Israel.

Notably, Eastern Libya’s recognition of Turkey’s maritime claims came the week that Netanyahu shared a map that showed the territory as “friendly” to Israel, the UAE and Greece.

Saddam Haftar even met in September with Netanyahu in the UAE, a Libyan source told MEE, confirming previous reporting. But Israel might see a wider Turkish claim to the Eastern Mediterranean pushing Greece closer into its orbit, one European official told MEE. 

The fact that Greece’s partners did not mobilise to prevent Eastern Libya’s ratification of the maritime deal shows just how much the Middle East is changing.

“Anyone can edit Wikipedia,” the adage goes. But, it turns out, a relatively small number actually do.

What is worthy of a digital page in the world’s largest and most-read encyclopedia is decided by roughly 270,000 active volunteers, enthusiasts who populate the online resource with information on anything from 19th-century medicine to TikTok trends. item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] 'There is no life left': How volunteers buried 600 bodies in Sudan's North Kordofan
item.description:
'There is no life left': How volunteers buried 600 bodies in Sudan's North Kordofan

Submitted by Mohammed Amin on Wed, 10/21/2026 - 07:30
Exclusive videos, photos and testimony reveal devastation left by massacres as Sudan's war continues
A volunteer buries a body in Bara, North Kordofan, Sudan (MEE)
Off

It took 50 volunteers to collect and bury more than 600 corpses.

The streets of Bara, in Sudan’s North Kordofan state, were lined with dead bodies. They were scattered in the surrounding villages. They were left on the road that links Bara to the state capital, the strategically vital city of el-Obeid.

Most of them were killed, eyewitnesses said, in revenge attacks carried out by the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF).

The pile-up of large numbers of dead bodies has turned Bara into a depopulated wasteland, its ground poisoned and beset by insects and scorpions. 

Unknown disease is spreading rapidly because of the corpses, with the volunteers, who wear protective suits and masks, working as hard as they can to dispose safely of the remains.

Videos and photos shared exclusively with Middle East Eye show the victims of massacres that took place during a period of intense fighting in July, when the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) took the area back from the RSF.

Multiple local sources, including activists and volunteers who participated in the process of retrieving and burying the dead, told MEE that most of the bodies were civilians. The rest were fighters, from both the SAF and RSF. 

On top of the more than 600 bodies that have been collected, the sources say there are hundreds more still left rotting in Bara and the surrounding countryside.

The activists, including the independent Emergency Response Rooms (ERRs), as well as volunteers from the popular resistance who have operated under the SAF’s command, accused the paramilitary RSF, which is sponsored by the United Arab Emirates and has been found by the UN and US to have committed genocide, of carrying out massacres and mass killings in the Bara area in October 2025.

Mass graves and exposed corpses

One volunteer told MEE that they had opened 200 mass graves in the area and then given a proper burial to all the corpses piled up inside. The source said that 400 other bodies had been buried.

“These efforts have been financed by many local groups including the women and men of Bara, as well as others in the diaspora, particularly those living in Gulf countries, and others in el-Obeid,” he explained. 

The Sudanese health ministry, Sudanese Red Crescent and other local initiatives provided the volunteers with cases and bags, the source said.

The group is still engaged in a process of cleaning and sanitisation in order not to spread disease. “We still need a lot of logistics and supplies including fuel, gloves, face masks, sanitisers, cases and bags, among other materials,” the volunteer said. 

“These corpses were found in the streets and squares as well as inside the houses,” Abdul Rahman, a leading member of the Bara resistance committee, told MEE.

“Others have been found in villages around Bara and the process is still ongoing as we believe that the number is higher than what we have from field reports.”

Abdul Rahman said there were hundreds of bodies still stranded in areas around Bara, including in Geraigikh, Jabrat al-Sheikh and Umm Syala.

The Sudanese information ministry has claimed that RSF violations have extended to more than 100 villages around Bara, with the area’s entire population having to flee their homes because of the attacks.

After a recent meeting between Bara’s local leaders and the Sudanese Information Minister Khalid Ismail Ahmed Ali el-Aisir, the ministry said the government would support victims of RSF violations by helping with medical care and reconstruction.

Bodies turned to skeletons

The photos and videos shared exclusively with MEE and published here show dead bodies that lay out in the open for months. 

Some of the bodies had decomposed, while others had already turned into skeletons, a process that can take just a few weeks in a hot climate like Sudan’s. 

Dozens of volunteers wearing gloves and protected uniforms collected the bodies, some of which had become simply a collection of bones. They packed them into old cars or pick-up trucks and buried them collectively. 

The skeletons were of all different ages, including children and elderly people. Other, fresher bodies were of military personnel.  

Volunteers described brutal conditions, dirty and poisoned ground beset by swarms of butterflies and other insects, visited by scorpions and littered with dead animals and birds.

"There is now no life left in Bara," one volunteer told MEE. The environment has totally collapsed because the vast number of dead bodies has resulted in the rapid spread of unknown diseases, they said.

“This work is hard, and we do it without direct help from the authorities or the international NGOs. The only thing we got are the mortuary bags from the Sudanese Red Crescent,” the volunteer said. 

“The majority of the corpses we have retrieved from Bara and other villages are civilians killed in revenge attacks in the city after the RSF entered it last year,” Ismail Karam Aldin, a volunteer and popular resistance member, told MEE over the phone.

“These efforts are only done by the volunteers of Bara’s people led by the popular resistance in the city. The Red Crescent and the local ministry of health have only provided the cases and bags to keep the corpses and bury them.” 

Sudan war continues along with external involvement

Sudan’s war began in April 2023 and is now the largest humanitarian crisis in the world, with over 11 million people forcibly displaced from their homes and at least 150,000 believed to be dead. 

Both the SAF and RSF have been accused of committing war crimes, while the RSF has been found to have carried out genocide in different parts of Darfur, western Sudan. 

The RSF is supported by the UAE, though Abu Dhabi continues to deny its involvement despite mounting evidence, including from the UN fact-finding mission for Sudan.   

On Monday, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu spoke in front of a map that divided Sudan between the RSF-held west, which was listed as being friendly to Israel and the UAE, and the rest of the country, which was listed as being friendly to Turkey, Saudi Arabia, Egypt and Pakistan. 

The SAF is supported militarily by Turkey and Egypt; the latter recently killed at least 114 people in an air strike on a gold mine on the Sudan-Egypt border.

In Sudan’s deserted Bara, blood waters its famous lemon trees
Read More »

North Kordofan has seen a wide SAF military advance in recent weeks, with the army taking control of Sodar, Um Badir, al-Mazroub and other areas, leaving most of the state back in its control.

A military source told MEE that the SAF would advance towards neighbouring West Kordofan state, particularly the cities of Al-Nuhud and Al-Khuwayyi, which are in regions rich in gum arabic. 

Previously, these areas produced more than 80 percent of the world’s gum arabic, an ingredient that is vital for multinational companies like Coca Cola and Pepsi and is also used in medicines in cosmetics.

For its part, the RSF has widened drone attacks on the entire country, including on el-Obeid, Kosti in White Nile state, Atbara in the north, the capital Khartoum and its twin city Omdurman. 

Diplomatic efforts to end the war continue to be ineffective.

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] Israel's vision of regional security rests on keeping Arab states weak
item.description:
Israel's vision of regional security rests on keeping Arab states weak

Submitted by Mohamad Elmasry on Mon, 10/19/2026 - 10:44
Six years after the Abraham Accords, a new report by a former Israeli intelligence chief outlines a doctrine treating peace deals as temporary and regional instability as an asset
Bahraini Foreign Minister Abdullatif al-Zayani, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, US President Donald Trump and UAE Foreign Minister Abdullah bin Zayed after signing the Abraham Accords at the White House on 15 September 2020 (Saul Loeb/AFP)
Off

The 2020 Abraham Accords did not bring a new era of regional peace, as US President Donald Trump promised. Instead, since the agreements were signed, Israel has carried out a genocide in Gaza and an unprecedented settlement expansion in the West Bank.

No one, least of all experts, is surprised.

From the moment the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain and Morocco formally normalised relations with Israel in 2020, the agreements - named the Abraham Accords by US President Donald Trump - were widely dismissed by critics as a farce.

Even before the accords were signed, Middle East experts argued that they represented an act of political theatre and deception, seemingly throwing the Palestinian cause under the bus while pretending to create peace and brotherhood between the "sons of Abraham".

Shortly before the signings, British-Palestinian academic Kamel Hawwash said the Israelis were taking the Emiratis "for a ride" that promised the continuation and acceleration of Israel's occupation and apartheid policies.

Around the same time, Joseph Massad, a professor of modern Arab politics, described the accords as a way of rewriting "the horrific colonial reality of Zionism and Israel in terms of religious and fraternal discord".

A new Israeli security report may provide important insights into Israel's strategic thinking when it signed the accords, as well as its policies in the years since.

Even before the accords were signed, Middle East experts argued that they represented an act of political theatre and deception

In the report, published on 12 October by Israel's Institute for National Security Studies (INSS), Tamir Hayman, a former head of Israeli military intelligence who now runs the institute, sets out what he calls Israel's "new security policy".

The report states that Israel does not view Arab countries as true nations, but instead as mere "collections of tribes and ethnic groups". As a result, undermining their stability "is viewed as a natural process" that Israel "should even encourage".

Indeed, the policy treats weak, fragmented Arab states as a source of security, since instability is something Israel "can manage more effectively than it can contend with strong nation-states".

It further defines Israel's approach as "perpetual preemptive war", with Israeli expansion - including into Syria and Lebanon - serving a broad objective of Arab "destabilization".

Destabilisation in practice

Hayman argues that Israel considers Middle East peace agreements as fundamentally "unattainable". When agreements are signed, they are "merely technical and temporary arrangements" designed to serve Israeli strategic objectives.

This is key to understanding not only how Israel approaches the Abraham Accords, but also its current regional posture, from Gaza and the West Bank to Syria and Lebanon.

Almost as soon as Syrians overthrew the longtime dictator Bashar al-Assad in December 2024, Israel started working to destabilise the country.

Israel's 'pilot zones' turn Lebanese sovereignty on its head
Belen Fernandez
Read More »

The Israeli military has reportedly carried out hundreds of attacks on Syrian territory, destroyed much of Syria's defence capabilities, occupied large swaths of territory and armed militia groups opposed to the new government.

In Lebanon, Israel has been arguably even more aggressive. There, it occupies between six percent and 20 percent of Lebanese territory.

Since signing a ceasefire agreement with Hezbollah in November 2024, Israel has repeatedly attacked Lebanon, killing thousands.

For the past several months, Israel has been engaged in peace talks with the Lebanese government. American mediators said in June that a tentative framework signed by Israeli and Lebanese leaders would lead to a "comprehensive peace" between the two countries.

The security doctrine outlined by Hayman, however, suggests that Israel may have signed the agreement as cover for continuing its occupation and further destabilising Lebanon. Indications are that Israel has no intention of withdrawing from the Lebanese territory it has occupied.

Hayman admits his report is partly subjective and that Israeli leadership has not formally acknowledged the new security doctrine he outlines.

Recent Israeli conduct, however, makes Hayman's analysis certainly plausible, if not probable. His background as former head of military intelligence adds weight to his interpretation.

A widening war

If Hayman's basic premises are accurate, the implications for the Middle East could be deeply troubling.

Israel may continue pursuing territorial expansion and Palestinian displacement in Gaza and the West Bank, while consolidating positions in Syria and Lebanon. Its confrontation with Iran could also escalate, with devastating consequences for the region.

The US-Israeli war on Iran has already generated significant chaos, including ongoing spillover into Yemen and Saudi Arabia.

Israel would welcome the Saudi-led war against Yemen's Houthis spreading further into the region, particularly if the widening conflict leads to additional destabilisation in important Arab countries.

In this context, Egypt's possible entry into the Yemen war on Saudi Arabia's side could serve Israeli strategic interests.

On 17 October, Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi requested parliamentary approval to provide military assistance to Saudi Arabia if Riyadh asks for it. Parliament has since postponed its vote until 26 October.

If Egypt does join the war, Israel could benefit in one of two ways.

On the one hand, the swift crushing of the Houthis would eliminate a threat to Israel and allow Israeli leaders to boast of the defeat as a successful extension of their 28 February attack on Iran.

On the other hand, if Egyptian help does not finish off the Houthis, the war could further widen. If nothing else, prolonged Egyptian involvement could drain resources and bog down a large, important Arab country on Israel's doorstep.

Furthermore, Israel's strategic partnership with the UAE deserves scrutiny. As I have previously argued, the two countries share interests in weakening and fragmenting Arab states. Both countries have supported non-state separatist actors across the region.

Normalisation as cover

Even the two countries that normalised relations with Israel decades ago - Egypt and Jordan - have reason to be concerned.

Since the start of the Gaza genocide, Israel has been accused of violating its Camp David agreement with Egypt. During the genocide, Israel took control of the Philadelphi Corridor, and more recently it has built new military fortifications in Rafah, a few kilometres from the Egyptian border.

Earlier this month, Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich issued an explicit threat to Egypt, warning that there would be "no Sinai" if it attacked Israel.

Arab governments seeking security through normalisation may instead be helping to undermine their own

Last year, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu expressed support for "Greater Israel", raising concerns in Jordan that Israel planned to expand beyond the Palestinian territories.

Despite all this, Arab governments continue to cooperate with Israel. Morocco upgraded its diplomatic relations with Israel last month, and Netanyahu travelled to the UAE in late September for talks that reportedly included officials from several other Arab countries.

Saudi Arabia, which appeared close to normalisation in 2023, continues to insist that it will not establish ties with Israel unless an independent Palestinian state is established.

Israeli media reported on 16 October, however, that Trump believes Saudi-Israeli normalisation is "back on the table". Israel's i24 news quoted Trump saying that Israel has provided assistance to Riyadh in its ongoing war against the Houthis in Yemen.

Why, then, would any Arab government contemplate engagement with Israel? Economic incentives, American pressure and security concerns undoubtedly help explain their calculations.

Normalisation, cooperation and meetings with Israel also offer Israel important diplomatic cover. Netanyahu has repeatedly argued that the Abraham Accords constitute evidence that Arab leaders do not care about the Palestinian cause and that some Arab leaders support Israel's war on Gaza.

What kind of peace can Arab governments expect from a state whose security doctrine treats neighbouring states' weakness as a strategic advantage?

The Abraham Accords were sold as a pathway to regional peace. Six years later, Hayman's analysis of Israel's security doctrine raises the possibility that Arab governments seeking security through normalisation may instead be helping to undermine their own.
